title: Book 2, Chapter 8 — Third Year of the War—Investment of Plataea—Naval Victories of Phormio—Thracian Irruption into Macedonia under Sitalces
paragraphs: The next summer the Peloponnesians and their allies did not invade Attica. They marched against Plataea instead, under Archidamus, son of Zeuxidamus, king of the Lacedaemonians. He had made camp and was about to lay waste the country when the Plataeans hurried to send envoys to him. They spoke as follows: “Archidamus and Lacedaemonians, in invading the territory of Plataea you do what is wrong in itself, and what is worthy neither of yourselves nor of the fathers who begot you. Pausanias, son of Cleombrotus, your countryman, freed Hellas from the Medes with the help of those Hellenes who were willing to share the risk of the battle fought near our city. Afterward he offered sacrifice to Zeus the Liberator in the marketplace of Plataea, called all the allies together, gave the Plataeans back their city and territory, and declared it independent and inviolate against aggression or conquest. If anyone attempted either, the allies present were to help as far as they could. Your fathers rewarded us in this way for the courage and patriotism we showed in that time of peril. You do just the opposite: you come with our bitterest enemies, the Thebans, to enslave us. We therefore appeal to the gods to whom the oaths were then sworn, to the gods of your ancestors, and finally to the gods of our own country. We call on you not to violate our territory or break the oaths, and to let us live independent, as Pausanias decreed.”

The Plataeans had got this far when Archidamus cut them short and said: “There is justice in what you say, Plataeans, if you act up to your words. Keep your independence, as Pausanias granted it. But join us in freeing your fellow countrymen who shared the perils of that time, joined in the oaths with you, and are now subject to the Athenians; for all this preparation and this war have been undertaken to free them and the rest. I could wish that you would share our labors and keep the oaths yourselves. If that is impossible, do what we have already asked of you: remain neutral and enjoy your own. Join neither side, but receive both as friends, and neither as allies for the war. With this we shall be satisfied.” Such were the words of Archidamus. The Plataeans heard him and went into the city. They told the people what had been said, and soon returned with the answer that they could not do what he proposed without consulting the Athenians, with whom their children and wives now were. They also had fears for the town: once he was gone, what was to prevent the Athenians from coming and taking it out of their hands? Or the Thebans, who would be included in the oaths, from using the proposed neutrality to make a second attempt to seize the city? Archidamus tried to reassure them on these points by saying: “You have only to hand over the city and houses to us Lacedaemonians, point out the boundaries of your land, the number of your fruit-trees, and whatever else can be counted, and withdraw yourselves wherever you like for as long as the war lasts. When it is over, we will give back to you whatever we received. In the meantime we will hold it in trust and keep it under cultivation, paying you a sufficient allowance.”

They heard him out and went back into the city. After consulting the people they said that they wished first to tell the Athenians of this proposal, and to accept it if the Athenians approved. In the meantime they asked him to grant them a truce and not to lay waste their territory. He granted a truce for the number of days needed for the journey, and in the meantime did not ravage their territory. The Plataean envoys went to Athens, consulted the Athenians, and came back with the following message for the people in the city: “The Athenians say, Plataeans, that since we became their allies they have never on any occasion abandoned us to an enemy, and that they will not neglect us now but will help us as far as they are able. They call on you, by the oaths your fathers swore, to keep the alliance unchanged.”

When the envoys delivered this message, the Plataeans resolved not to be unfaithful to the Athenians. If it must be, they would endure the sight of their lands laid waste and any other trials that might come. They would send out no more envoys, and would answer from the wall that they could not do what the Lacedaemonians proposed. As soon as he received this answer, King Archidamus first made a solemn appeal to the gods and heroes of the country, in these words: “Gods and heroes of the Plataean territory, be my witnesses. We did not invade this land as aggressors in the first place, but only after these people had abandoned the common oath. In this land our fathers offered you their prayers before defeating the Medes, and you made it favorable to the Hellenic arms. Nor shall we be aggressors in the measures we may now take, since we have made many fair proposals and have not succeeded. Grant in your kindness that those who were the first to offend may be punished for it, and that those who would inflict vengeance rightly may obtain it.”

After this appeal to the gods Archidamus set his army in motion. First he enclosed the town with a palisade made of the fruit-trees they cut down, to stop any further exit from Plataea. Next they threw up a mound against the city, hoping that the size of the force at work would bring about a quick reduction of the place. They cut timber from Cithaeron and built it up on either side, laying it like lattice-work to form a wall that would keep the mound from spreading. They carried to it wood and stones and earth and any other material that would help to complete it. They worked at the mound for seventy days and nights without a break. They were divided into relief parties, so that some carried while others slept and ate, and the Lacedaemonian officer attached to each contingent kept the men at the work. But the Plataeans watched the progress of the mound. They built a wall of wood and fixed it on that part of the city wall against which the mound was being raised, and inside it they built up bricks taken from the neighboring houses. The timbers bound the structure together and kept it from growing weak as it rose in height. It also had a covering of skins and hides, which protected the woodwork against burning missiles and let the men work in safety. So the wall was raised to a great height, and the mound opposite rose no less quickly. The Plataeans also thought of another device: they pulled out part of the wall where the mound rested against it, and carried the earth into the city.

When the Peloponnesians discovered this, they twisted clay into wattles of reed and threw them into the breach in the mound, to give it firmness and keep it from being carried away like the soil. Blocked in this way, the Plataeans changed their method. They dug a mine from the town, calculated their way under the mound, and began to carry off its material as before. For a long while the enemy outside did not find this out, so that for all they threw on top, their mound made no matching progress: it was being carried away from beneath and kept settling into the empty space. But the Plataeans feared that even so they might not be able to hold out against the superior numbers of the enemy, and they had yet another invention. They stopped working at the large building in front of the mound. Starting at either end of it from the old low wall, they built a new wall inside, in the form of a crescent curving in toward the town. Their purpose was this: if the great wall were taken, the crescent would remain, and the enemy would have to throw up a fresh mound against it. As they advanced inside, they would not only have their trouble over again but would also be exposed to missiles on their flanks. While raising the mound the Peloponnesians also brought up engines against the city. One of these was brought up on the mound against the great building and shook down a good piece of it, to the no small alarm of the Plataeans. Others were advanced against different parts of the wall, but the Plataeans lassoed them and broke them. They also hung great beams by long iron chains from either end of two poles laid on the wall and projecting over it. Whenever the engine threatened any point, they drew the beams up at an angle, then let go and let the beam drop with its chains slack. It fell with a run and snapped off the nose of the battering ram.

After this the Peloponnesians found that their engines achieved nothing and that their mound was met by the counterwork. They concluded that their present means of attack were not enough to take the city, and prepared to build a wall around it. First, however, they decided to try fire and see whether, with the help of a wind, they could burn the town, since it was not a large one. Indeed they thought of every possible way in which the place might be reduced without the expense of a blockade. They brought faggots of brushwood and threw them from the mound, first into the space between it and the wall. This soon filled up, because so many hands were at work, and they then heaped the faggots as far into the town as they could reach from the top. They lit the wood by setting fire to it with sulphur and pitch. The result was a fire greater than anyone had ever yet seen produced by human agency, though it could not of course be compared with the spontaneous fires that sometimes occur when the wind rubs the branches of a mountain forest together. This fire was remarkable not only for its size. At the end of so many perils it came within an ace of destroying the Plataeans: a great part of the town became entirely inaccessible, and if a wind had blown on it, as the enemy hoped, nothing could have saved them. As it was, there is also a story that heavy rain and thunder came on, put the fire out, and averted the danger.

Having failed in this last attempt, the Peloponnesians left a part of their forces on the spot and dismissed the rest. They built a wall of circumvallation around the town, dividing the ground among the various cities present, with a ditch made inside and outside the lines, from which they got their bricks. Everything was finished by about the rising of Arcturus. They left men enough to man half the wall, the Boeotians manning the rest, and drew off their army, which dispersed to the several cities. The Plataeans had earlier sent their wives and children and oldest men, and the mass of the non-combatants, to Athens. So the besieged left in the place numbered four hundred of their own citizens, eighty Athenians, and a hundred and ten women to bake their bread. This was the total at the start of the siege, and there was no one else within the walls, slave or free. Such were the arrangements made for the blockade of Plataea.

The same summer, at the same time as the expedition against Plataea, the Athenians marched against the Chalcidians in the direction of Thrace, and against the Bottiaeans, just as the corn was getting ripe. They had two thousand heavy infantry and two hundred horse, under Xenophon, son of Euripides, with two colleagues. They came to Spartolus in Bottiaea and destroyed the corn. They also had some hope that the city would come over through the intrigues of a faction inside. But those of a different mind had sent to Olynthus, and a garrison of heavy infantry and other troops arrived. These came out of Spartolus and were engaged by the Athenians in front of the town. The Chalcidian heavy infantry, and some auxiliaries with them, were beaten and retreated into Spartolus. But the Chalcidian horse and light troops defeated the horse and light troops of the Athenians. The Chalcidians already had a few targeteers from Crusis, and soon after the battle they were joined by others from Olynthus. When the light troops from Spartolus saw them, they were emboldened by this reinforcement and by their earlier success. With the help of the Chalcidian horse and the troops just arrived, they attacked the Athenians again, and the Athenians retired upon the two divisions they had left with their baggage. Whenever the Athenians advanced, their adversary gave way, and whenever they began to retire, he pressed them with missiles. The Chalcidian horse also rode up and charged them just as they pleased, and at last caused a panic among them, routed them, and pursued them a great distance. The Athenians took refuge in Potidæa, later recovered their dead under truce, and returned to Athens with the remnant of their army. Four hundred and thirty men and all the generals had fallen. The Chalcidians and Bottiaeans set up a trophy, took up their dead, and dispersed to their several cities.

The same summer, not long after this, the Ambraciots and Chaonians wanted to reduce the whole of Acarnania and detach it from Athens. They persuaded the Lacedaemonians to equip a fleet from their confederacy and send a thousand heavy infantry to Acarnania. They argued that if a combined movement were made by land and sea, the coast Acarnanians would be unable to march. The conquest of Zacynthus and Cephallenia would then easily follow the possession of Acarnania, and the cruise around Peloponnese would no longer be so convenient for the Athenians. Besides this, there was a hope of taking Naupactus. The Lacedaemonians at once sent off a few vessels, with the heavy infantry on board, under Cnemus, who was still high admiral. They also sent round orders for the fleet to equip as quickly as possible and sail to Leucas. The Corinthians were the most forward in the business, since the Ambraciots were a colony of theirs. The ships from Corinth, Sicyon, and the neighborhood were getting ready, and those from Leucas, Anactorium, and Ambracia, which had arrived earlier, were waiting for them at Leucas. Meanwhile Cnemus and his thousand heavy infantry had run into the gulf, giving the slip to Phormio, the commander of the Athenian squadron stationed off Naupactus, and began at once to prepare for the land expedition. The Hellenic troops with him were the Ambraciots, Leucadians, and Anactorians, and the thousand Peloponnesians he had brought. The barbarians were a thousand Chaonians. They belong to a nation that has no king, and were led by Photys and Nicanor, the two members of the royal family to whom the chieftainship for that year had been entrusted. With the Chaonians came also some Thesprotians, who likewise have no king, and some Molossians and Atintanians led by Sabylinthus, the guardian of King Tharyps, who was still a minor. There were also some Paravaeans under their king Oroedus, accompanied by a thousand Orestians, subjects of King Antiochus, whom he had placed under the command of Oroedus. There were also a thousand Macedonians sent by Perdiccas without the knowledge of the Athenians, but they arrived too late. With this force Cnemus set out, without waiting for the fleet from Corinth. They passed through the territory of Amphilochian Argos and sacked the open village of Limnaea. They then advanced to Stratus, the Acarnanian capital. They felt convinced that once it was taken, the rest of the country would quickly follow.

The Acarnanians found themselves invaded by a large army by land and threatened from the sea by a hostile fleet. They made no combined attempt at resistance but stayed to defend their homes, and sent for help to Phormio. He replied that with a fleet on the point of sailing from Corinth, he could not leave Naupactus unprotected. Meanwhile the Peloponnesians and their allies advanced on Stratus in three divisions. They intended to encamp near it and to try the wall by force if negotiation failed. The order of march was as follows. The Chaonians and the rest of the barbarians held the center, the Leucadians and Anactorians and their followers were on the right, and Cnemus with the Peloponnesians and Ambraciots was on the left. Each division was a long way from the others, and sometimes even out of sight of them. The Hellenes advanced in good order, keeping a look-out, until they encamped in a good position. But the Chaonians were full of self-confidence and had the highest reputation for courage among the tribes of that part of the continent. They did not wait to occupy their camp but rushed on with the rest of the barbarians, thinking that they would take the town by assault and win the sole glory of the enterprise. While they were coming on, the Stratians saw how things stood. They thought that the defeat of this division would greatly dishearten the Hellenes behind it, so they filled the surroundings of the town with ambuscades. As soon as the Chaonians approached, they engaged them at close quarters from the city and from the ambuscades. A panic seized the Chaonians and great numbers of them were killed. As soon as they were seen to give way, the rest of the barbarians turned and fled. Because their allies had gone so far ahead, neither of the Hellenic divisions knew anything of the battle, and they supposed that the others were hurrying on to encamp. However, when the fleeing barbarians broke in upon them, they opened their ranks to receive them, brought their divisions together, and stayed where they were for the day. The Stratians did not offer to engage them, since the rest of the Acarnanians had not yet arrived, but contented themselves with slinging at them from a distance. This distressed them greatly, as there was no moving without their armor. The Acarnanians seem to excel in this mode of warfare.

As soon as night fell, Cnemus hastily drew off his army to the river Anapus, about nine miles from Stratus. The next day he recovered his dead under truce, and was joined there by the friendly Oeniadae. He fell back upon their city before the enemy’s reinforcements came up. From there each force returned home, and the Stratians set up a trophy for the battle with the barbarians.

Meanwhile the fleet from Corinth and the rest of the confederates in the Crissaean Gulf was supposed to co-operate with Cnemus and prevent the coast Acarnanians from joining their countrymen in the interior. It was prevented from doing so, because about the time of the battle at Stratus it was forced to fight Phormio and the twenty Athenian vessels stationed at Naupactus. Phormio had been watching them as they coasted out of the gulf, and wished to attack them in the open sea. But the Corinthians and their allies had started for Acarnania with no idea of fighting at sea, in vessels more like transports for carrying soldiers. Besides, they never dreamed that the twenty Athenian ships would dare to engage their forty-seven. However, while they were coasting along their own shore, the Athenians sailed along in line with them. And when they tried to cross from Patrae in Achaea to the mainland on the other side, on their way to Acarnania, they saw the Athenians coming out again from Chalcis and the river Evenus to meet them. They slipped their moorings in the night, but were observed, and were at length forced to fight in mid passage. Each state that contributed to the armament had its own general. The Corinthian commanders were Machaon, Isocrates, and Agatharchidas. The Peloponnesians ranged their vessels in as large a circle as possible without leaving an opening, with the prows outside and the sterns in. Inside it they placed all the small craft that accompanied them, and their five best sailers, ready to dash out at a moment’s notice and reinforce any point the enemy threatened.

The Athenians, formed in line, sailed round and round them. By continually brushing past, and making as though they would attack at once, they forced them to contract their circle. Phormio had earlier cautioned them not to attack until he gave the signal. His hope was that the Peloponnesians would not keep their order as a force on shore would, but that the ships would fall foul of one another and the small craft would cause confusion. If the wind should blow from the gulf, he felt sure they would not remain steady for an instant. (He kept sailing round them in expectation of this wind, which usually rose toward morning.) He also thought that it rested with him to attack when he pleased, as his ships were better sailers, and that an attack timed by the coming of the wind would tell best. When the wind came down, the enemy’s ships were in a narrow space, and between the wind and the small craft dashing against them they at once fell into confusion. Ship fell foul of ship, and the crews pushed them off with poles. Their shouting, swearing, and struggling with one another made the captains’ orders and the boatswains’ cries alike inaudible. And because they lacked the practice to clear their oars in the rough water, the vessels did not obey their helmsmen properly. At this moment Phormio gave the signal, and the Athenians attacked. They first sank one of the admirals, and then disabled every ship they came across. In the confusion no one thought of resistance, and they fled for Patrae and Dyme in Achaea. The Athenians gave chase and captured twelve ships. They took most of the men out of them and sailed to Molycrium. There they set up a trophy on the promontory of Rhium and dedicated a ship to Poseidon, and then returned to Naupactus. As for the Peloponnesians, they at once sailed with their remaining ships along the coast from Dyme and Patrae to Cyllene, the Eleian arsenal. There Cnemus also arrived after the battle at Stratus, together with the ships from Leucas that were to have joined them.

The Lacedaemonians now sent three commissioners to the fleet of Cnemus: Timocrates, Brasidas, and Lycophron. Their orders were to prepare to engage again with better fortune, and not to be driven from the sea by a few vessels. The Lacedaemonians could not at all account for their defeat, the less so as it was their first attempt at sea. They fancied that their navy was not so inferior, but that there had been misconduct somewhere. They did not consider the long experience of the Athenians compared with the little practice they had had themselves. The commissioners were therefore sent in anger. As soon as they arrived, they set to work with Cnemus to order ships from the different states and to put those they already had in fighting order. Meanwhile Phormio sent word to Athens of their preparations and of his own victory. He asked that as many ships as possible be sent to him quickly, as he expected a battle any day. Twenty were sent, but their commander was instructed to go to Crete first. Nicias, a Cretan of Gortys, who was proxenus of the Athenians, had persuaded them to sail against Cydonia, promising to bring about the reduction of that hostile town. His real wish was to oblige the Polichnitans, neighbors of the Cydonians. So he went with the ships to Crete and, accompanied by the Polichnitans, laid waste the lands of the Cydonians. Between adverse winds and stress of weather he wasted no little time there.

While the Athenians were detained in Crete in this way, the Peloponnesians in Cyllene got ready for battle and coasted along to Panormus in Achaea, where their land army had come to support them. Phormio also coasted along to Molycrian Rhium and anchored outside it with twenty ships, the same he had fought with before. This Rhium was friendly to the Athenians. The other Rhium, in Peloponnese, lies opposite to it. The sea between them is about three-quarters of a mile broad and forms the mouth of the Crissaean gulf. When the Peloponnesians saw the Athenians anchor, they cast anchor at the Achaean Rhium, not far from Panormus, where their army lay, with seventy-seven ships. For six or seven days they remained opposite each other, practicing and preparing for the battle. The Peloponnesians were resolved not to sail out of the Rhia into the open sea, for fear of a repeat of the disaster that had already happened to them. The Athenians were resolved not to sail into the straits, thinking that fighting in the narrows was to the enemy’s advantage. At last Cnemus and Brasidas and the rest of the Peloponnesian commanders wanted to bring on a battle as soon as possible, before reinforcements should arrive from Athens. They noticed that most of the men were cowed by the previous defeat and out of heart for the business. So they first called them together and encouraged them as follows:

“Peloponnesians, the late engagement may have made some of you afraid of the one now in prospect, but it really gives no just ground for apprehension. There was little enough preparation for it, as you know, and the object of our voyage was not so much to fight at sea as to make an expedition by land. Besides this, the chances of war were largely against us, and perhaps inexperience also had something to do with our failure in our first naval action. It was not cowardice, therefore, that produced our defeat. Nor ought a determination that force has not crushed, but that still has a word to say to its adversary, to lose its edge because of an accident. We should admit the possibility of a chance miscarriage, but we should also know that brave hearts must always be brave, and that while they remain so they can never offer inexperience as an excuse for misconduct. Nor are you so far behind the enemy in experience as you are ahead of him in courage. The science of your opponents, if valor accompanied it, would also have the presence of mind to carry out the lesson it has learnt in an emergency. But a faint heart will make all art powerless in the face of danger. For fear takes away presence of mind, and without valor art is useless. Set your superior daring against their superior experience, and set against the fear induced by defeat the fact that you were unprepared then. Remember, too, that you always have the advantage of superior numbers, and of engaging off your own coast, supported by your heavy infantry. As a rule, numbers and equipment give victory. At no point, therefore, is defeat likely. As for our previous mistakes, the very fact that they occurred will teach us better for the future. Steersmen and sailors may therefore attend with confidence to their several duties, none leaving the station assigned to him. As for ourselves, we promise to prepare for the engagement at least as well as your previous commanders did, and to give no excuse for anyone to misconduct himself. Should anyone insist on doing so, he shall meet with the punishment he deserves, while the brave shall be honored with the appropriate rewards of valor.”

The Peloponnesian commanders encouraged their men in this fashion. Phormio, meanwhile, was himself not without fears for the courage of his men. He noticed that they were forming groups among themselves and were alarmed at the odds against them, and he wished to call them together and give them confidence and counsel for the present emergency. He had often told them before, and had accustomed their minds to the idea, that there was no numerical superiority they could not face. And the men themselves had long been persuaded that Athenians need never retire before any quantity of Peloponnesian vessels. At the moment, however, he saw that the sight before them had dispirited them. Wishing to restore their confidence, he called them together and spoke as follows:

“I see, my men, that the number of the enemy frightens you, and so I have called you together. I do not like to see you afraid of what is not really terrible. First, the Peloponnesians were already defeated, and they do not themselves think they are a match for us. That is why they have not dared to meet us on equal terms and have fitted out this crowd of ships against us. Next, there is the quality they rely on most, the courage they suppose to be natural to them. Their confidence here comes only from the success that experience in land service usually gives them, and they imagine it will do the same for them at sea. But if that advantage is theirs on land, in all justice it is ours on this element. They are not superior to us in courage; we are simply more confident, each of us, in the department where we have experience. Besides, the Lacedaemonians use their supremacy over their allies to advance their own glory, and most of those allies are being brought into danger against their will. Otherwise they would never have risked a fresh engagement after so decided a defeat. You need not, therefore, fear their dash. You, on the contrary, inspire in them a much greater and better founded alarm, both because of your recent victory and because they believe we would not stand against them unless we were about to do something worthy of so signal a success. An adversary who is superior in numbers, like the one before us, goes into action trusting more to strength than to resolution. But a man who of his own choice faces tremendous odds must have very great inner resources to draw upon. For these reasons the Peloponnesians fear our irrational audacity more than they would ever have feared a more proportionate preparation. Besides, many armaments have before now succumbed to an inferior force through want of skill, or sometimes of courage, and we have neither of these defects. As for the battle, if I can help it, it shall not be fought in the strait, and I will not sail in there at all. In a contest between a number of clumsily handled vessels and a small, fast, well-handled squadron, lack of sea room is an undoubted disadvantage. One cannot ram an enemy properly without seeing him a good way off, nor can one retire when pressed if need be. One can neither break through the line nor turn back on the enemy’s rear, which are the proper tactics for a fast sailer. Instead the naval action necessarily becomes a land battle, and in that numbers must decide the matter. I will provide against all this as far as I can. Stay at your posts by your ships, and be quick to catch the word of command, the more so because we are watching one another from so short a distance. In action, regard order and silence as all-important — they are useful in war generally, and in naval engagements in particular — and conduct yourselves before the enemy in a manner worthy of your past exploits. The issues you will fight for are great: to destroy the naval hopes of the Peloponnesians, or to bring the Athenians’ fears for the sea nearer to them. And I remind you once more that you have already defeated most of these men, and beaten men do not face a danger a second time with the same determination.”

This was Phormio’s exhortation. The Peloponnesians saw that the Athenians would not sail into the gulf and the narrows, and they wanted to draw them in whether they wished it or not. So at dawn they put out, formed four abreast, and sailed inside the gulf toward their own country, with the right wing leading, as they had lain at anchor. In this wing they placed twenty of their best sailers. Their purpose was this: if Phormio thought they were aiming at Naupactus and coasted along to save the place, the Athenians would be unable to escape their attack by getting outside their wing, and the twenty ships would cut them off. Things turned out as they expected. Phormio was alarmed for the place, which was at that moment empty of its garrison, and as soon as he saw them put out, he embarked reluctantly and in haste and sailed along the shore, while the Messenian land forces moved along to support him. The Peloponnesians saw him coasting in single file, and therefore inside the gulf and close inshore, just as they had wished. At one signal they turned suddenly and bore down in line at their best speed on the Athenians, hoping to cut off the whole squadron. The eleven leading ships escaped the Peloponnesian wing and its sudden movement and reached the more open water. But the rest were overtaken as they tried to run through, driven ashore and disabled, and the crews who had not swum out of them were slain. The Peloponnesians lashed some of the ships to their own and towed them off empty, and one they took with its men in it. Others were just being towed away when the Messenians saved them by dashing into the sea in their armor and fighting from the decks they had boarded.

So far victory was with the Peloponnesians, and the Athenian fleet was destroyed. Meanwhile the twenty ships of the right wing were chasing the eleven Athenian ships that had escaped the sudden movement and reached the more open water. All of these but one outsailed their pursuers and got safely into Naupactus. They formed close inshore opposite the temple of Apollo, with their prows facing the enemy, and prepared to defend themselves if the Peloponnesians should sail inshore against them. After a while the Peloponnesians came up, chanting the paean for their victory as they sailed. The one remaining Athenian ship was being chased by a Leucadian ship far ahead of the rest. But a merchantman happened to be lying at anchor in the roadstead, and the Athenian ship had time to sail around it, strike the pursuing Leucadian amidships, and sink her. This exploit was so sudden and unexpected that it caused a panic among the Peloponnesians. They had fallen out of order in the excitement of victory, and some of them dropped their oars and stopped their way to let the main body come up, which was an unsafe thing to do with the enemy’s prows so near. Others ran aground in the shallows, because they did not know the waters.

The Athenians were elated at this incident. At one word they gave a cheer and dashed at the enemy. He was embarrassed by his mistakes and the disorder he found himself in, and he stood for only an instant before fleeing to Panormus, from which he had put out. The Athenians followed on his heels and took the six ships nearest them. They also recovered those of their own that had been disabled close inshore and taken in tow at the beginning of the action. They killed some of the crews and took some prisoners. On board the Leucadian ship that went down off the merchantman was the Lacedaemonian Timocrates, who killed himself when the ship was sunk, and his body was cast up in the harbor of Naupactus. On their return the Athenians set up a trophy on the spot from which they had put out and turned the day. They picked up the wrecks and the dead that were on their shore and gave the enemy his dead back under truce. The Peloponnesians also set up a trophy as victors, for the defeat they had inflicted on the ships they had disabled inshore, and they dedicated the ship they had taken at Achaean Rhium beside the trophy. After this, fearing the reinforcement expected from Athens, all except the Leucadians sailed into the Crissaean Gulf for Corinth. Not long after their retreat, the twenty Athenian ships that were to have joined Phormio before the battle arrived at Naupactus.

So the summer ended. Winter was now at hand. The fleet had retired to Corinth and the Crissaean Gulf, and Cnemus, Brasidas and the other Peloponnesian captains dispersed it. The Megarians then persuaded them to attempt Piraeus, the port of Athens, which had naturally been left unguarded and open because of Athens’ decided superiority at sea. Their plan was as follows. Each man was to take his oar, cushion and rowlock thong, go overland from Corinth to the sea on the Athenian side, get to Megara as quickly as he could, launch the forty ships that happened to be in the docks at Nisaea, and sail at once to Piraeus. There was no fleet on the lookout in the harbor, and no one had the least idea that the enemy would attempt a surprise. An open attack, it was thought, would never be ventured on deliberately, or, if it were contemplated, would soon be known at Athens. Once the plan was formed, the next step was to carry it out. They arrived by night and launched the ships from Nisaea. But they did not sail to Piraeus, as they had originally intended, because they were afraid of the risk (there was also some talk of a wind having stopped them). They sailed instead to the point of Salamis that looks toward Megara, where there was a fort and a squadron of three ships to prevent anything from sailing in or out of Megara. They assaulted this fort and towed off the galleys empty. They took the inhabitants by surprise and began to lay waste the rest of the island.

Meanwhile fire signals were raised to alarm Athens, and a panic followed there as serious as any during the war. In the city they thought that the enemy had already sailed into Piraeus. In Piraeus they thought that Salamis had been taken and that the enemy might arrive in the port at any moment. And that could easily have happened if their hearts had been a little firmer, for certainly no wind would have prevented it. As soon as day broke, the Athenians assembled in full force, launched their ships, embarked in haste and uproar, and went with the fleet to Salamis, while their soldiers mounted guard in Piraeus. The Peloponnesians learned that relief was coming. By then they had overrun most of Salamis, and they hastily sailed off to Nisaea with their plunder, their captives and the three ships from Fort Budorum. The state of their ships also caused them some anxiety, since it was a long time since they had been launched and they were not watertight. Once they reached Megara, they went back to Corinth on foot. The Athenians found them no longer at Salamis and sailed back. After this they made arrangements for guarding Piraeus more carefully in the future, by closing the harbors and by other suitable precautions.

About the same time, at the beginning of this winter, Sitalces, son of Teres, the Odrysian king of Thrace, made an expedition against Perdiccas, son of Alexander, king of Macedonia, and against the Chalcidians in the neighborhood of Thrace. His object was to enforce one promise and fulfill another. On the one hand, Perdiccas had made him a promise when he was hard pressed at the beginning of the war. The condition was that Sitalces should reconcile the Athenians to him and not try to restore his brother and enemy, the pretender Philip. But Perdiccas had not offered to keep his engagement. On the other hand, Sitalces himself, when he entered into alliance with the Athenians, had agreed to put an end to the Chalcidian war in Thrace. These were the two objects of his invasion. He brought with him Amyntas, the son of Philip, whom he meant for the throne of Macedonia, and some Athenian envoys who were then at his court on this business, and Hagnon as general. The Athenians were to join him against the Chalcidians with a fleet and as many soldiers as they could get together.

He began with the Odrysians and first called out the Thracian tribes subject to him between Mounts Haemus and Rhodope and the Euxine and Hellespont. Next he called the Getae beyond Haemus and the other hordes settled south of the Danube near the Euxine. Like the Getae, these border on the Scythians and are armed in the same manner, all of them being mounted archers. Besides these he summoned many of the independent hill Thracians, swordsmen called Dii, who mostly live on Mount Rhodope. Some of them came as mercenaries and others as volunteers. He also summoned the Agrianes and Laeaeans and the rest of the Paeonian tribes in his empire. These lay at its confines, which extended up to the Laeaean Paeonians and the river Strymon, which flows from Mount Scombrus through the country of the Agrianes and Laeaeans. There the empire of Sitalces ends and the territory of the independent Paeonians begins. Bordering on the Triballi, who are also independent, were the Treres and Tilataeans, who live to the north of Mount Scombrus and extend toward the setting sun as far as the river Oskius. This river rises in the same mountains as the Nestus and Hebrus, a wild and extensive range connected with Rhodope.

The empire of the Odrysians extended along the seaboard from Abdera to the mouth of the Danube in the Euxine. By the shortest route, a merchantman with a wind astern the whole way takes four days and four nights to sail this coast. By land, an active man traveling by the shortest road can get from Abdera to the Danube in eleven days. Such was the length of its coast line. Inland, from Byzantium to the Laeaeans and the Strymon, which was the farthest limit of its extension into the interior, it is a journey of thirteen days for an active man. The tribute from all the barbarian districts and the Hellenic cities amounted to about four hundred talents in gold and silver. This is counting what they brought in under Seuthes, the successor of Sitalces, who raised it to its greatest height. There were also presents in gold and silver of no less value, besides stuff, plain and embroidered, and other articles, made not only for the king but also for the Odrysian lords and nobles. For a custom was established here that is the opposite of the one in the Persian kingdom, namely of taking rather than giving. More disgrace was attached to not giving when asked than to asking and being refused. This custom prevailed elsewhere in Thrace, but it was practiced most extensively among the powerful Odrysians, since it was impossible to get anything done without a present. It was thus a very powerful kingdom. In revenue and general prosperity it surpassed all the nations in Europe between the Ionian Gulf and the Euxine, and in numbers and military resources it came decidedly next to the Scythians. No people in Europe can bear comparison with the Scythians, and not even in Asia is there any single nation that would be a match for them if they were unanimous. Of course they are not on a level with other races in general intelligence and the arts of civilized life.

The master of this empire was now preparing to take the field. When everything was ready, he set out on his march for Macedonia. He went first through his own dominions, and next over the desolate range of Cercine, which divides the Sintians and Paeonians. He crossed by a road that he had made on a former campaign against the Paeonians, by felling the timber. Passing over these mountains, with the Paeonians on his right and the Sintians and Maedians on his left, he finally arrived at Doberus, in Paeonia. He lost none of his army on the march, except perhaps by sickness, and he even received some additions, since many of the independent Thracians volunteered to join him in the hope of plunder. The whole is said to have formed a grand total of a hundred and fifty thousand. Most of this was infantry, though about a third was cavalry, furnished principally by the Odrysians themselves and next to them by the Getae. The most warlike of the infantry were the independent swordsmen who came down from Rhodope. The rest of the mixed multitude that followed him was formidable chiefly by its numbers.

They assembled at Doberus and prepared to descend from the heights upon Lower Macedonia, where the dominions of Perdiccas lay. The Lyncestae, the Elimiots and other tribes farther inland are Macedonians by blood, and allies and dependants of their kindred, but they still have their own separate governments. The country on the sea coast, now called Macedonia, was first acquired by Alexander, the father of Perdiccas, and his ancestors, who were originally Temenids from Argos. They did this by expelling the Pierians from Pieria. The Pierians afterwards lived at Phagres and other places under Mount Pangaeus, beyond the Strymon (indeed the country between Pangaeus and the sea is still called the Pierian Gulf). They also expelled the Bottiaeans, now neighbors of the Chalcidians, from Bottia, and they acquired in Paeonia a narrow strip along the river Axius, extending to Pella and the sea. The district of Mygdonia, between the Axius and the Strymon, was also added, by the expulsion of the Edonians. From Eordia they drove the Eordians, most of whom perished, though a few of them still live around Physca, and from Almopia they drove the Almopians. These Macedonians also conquered places belonging to the other tribes, which are still theirs: Anthemus, Crestonia, Bisaltia, and much of Macedonia proper. The whole is now called Macedonia, and at the time of the invasion of Sitalces, Perdiccas, Alexander’s son, was the reigning king.

These Macedonians could not take the field against so numerous an invader, and they shut themselves up in such strong places and fortresses as the country possessed. There were not many of these. Most of those now found in the country were built afterwards by Archelaus, the son of Perdiccas, when he came to the throne. He also cut straight roads and otherwise put the kingdom on a better footing, in horses, heavy infantry and other war material, than all the eight kings before him had done. The Thracian host advanced from Doberus and first invaded what had once been Philip’s government. It took Idomene by assault, and Gortynia, Atalanta and some other places by negotiation, these last coming over out of love for Philip’s son Amyntas, who was then with Sitalces. Sitalces laid siege to Europus and failed to take it. He then advanced into the rest of Macedonia, to the left of Pella and Cyrrhus. He did not go beyond this into Bottiaea and Pieria, but stayed to lay waste Mygdonia, Crestonia and Anthemus.

The Macedonians never even thought of meeting him with infantry. But their horse had been reinforced from their allies in the interior, and as opportunity offered, small bodies of it attacked the Thracian host. They wore cuirasses and were excellent horsemen. Wherever they charged, they overthrew everything before them, but they ran considerable risk of entangling themselves in the masses of the enemy. So they finally gave up these efforts, deciding that they were not strong enough to venture against such superior numbers.

Meanwhile Sitalces opened negotiations with Perdiccas on the objects of his expedition. The Athenians did not believe that he would come, and they did not appear with their fleet, though they sent presents and envoys. Finding this, he dispatched a large part of his army against the Chalcidians and Bottiaeans. He shut them up inside their walls and laid waste their country. While he remained in these parts, the people farther south, such as the Thessalians, the Magnetes, the other tribes subject to the Thessalians, and the Hellenes as far as Thermopylae, all feared that the army might advance against them, and made their preparations. The Thracians beyond the Strymon to the north, who inhabited the plains, shared these fears. These were the Panaeans, the Odomanti, the Droi and the Dersaeans, all of whom are independent. It was even a matter of conversation among the Hellenes who were enemies of Athens whether he might not be invited by his ally to advance against them also. Meanwhile he held Chalcidice, Bottice and Macedonia and was ravaging them all. But he found that he was not succeeding in any of the objects of his invasion, and that his army was without provisions and suffering from the severity of the season. So he listened to the advice of Seuthes, son of Spardacus, his nephew and highest officer, and decided to retreat without delay. Perdiccas had secretly gained this Seuthes by the promise of his sister in marriage with a rich dowry. In accordance with this advice, and after a stay of thirty days in all, eight of which were spent in Chalcidice, Sitalces retired home as quickly as he could. Perdiccas afterwards gave his sister Stratonice to Seuthes, as he had promised. Such was the history of the expedition of Sitalces.

In the course of this winter, after the Peloponnesian fleet had dispersed, the Athenians in Naupactus under Phormio coasted along to Astacus, disembarked, and marched into the interior of Acarnania with four hundred Athenian heavy infantry and four hundred Messenians. They expelled some suspected persons from Stratus, Coronta and other places, and restored Cynes, son of Theolytus, to Coronta. Then they returned to their ships. They decided that it was impossible, in the winter season, to march against Oeniadae, a place that, unlike the rest of Acarnania, had always been hostile to them. The river Achelous flows from Mount Pindus through Dolopia and the country of the Agraeans and Amphilochians and the plain of Acarnania, passing the town of Stratus in its upper course. Where it falls into the sea around Oeniadae, it forms lakes, and so makes the place impracticable for an army in winter because of the water. Opposite Oeniadae lie most of the islands called Echinades, so close to the mouths of the Achelous that this powerful stream is constantly forming deposits against them. It has already joined some of the islands to the mainland, and seems likely before long to do the same with the rest. The current is strong, deep and muddy, and the islands are so thick together that they trap the deposit and prevent it from dispersing. They lie not in one line but irregularly, so as to leave no direct passage for the water into the open sea. The islands in question are uninhabited and of no great size. There is also a story that Alcmaeon, son of Amphiaraus, during his wanderings after the murder of his mother, was told by Apollo to settle in this spot. The oracle intimated that he would have no release from his terrors until he found a country to live in that had not been seen by the sun, and had not existed as land, at the time he slew his mother. All else was to him polluted ground. The story goes on to say that he was perplexed by this, until at last he noticed this deposit of the Achelous. He considered that a place large enough to support life might have been thrown up during the long interval since his mother’s death and the beginning of his wanderings. So he settled in the district around Oeniadae, founded a dominion, and left the country its name from his son Acarnan. Such is the story we have received about Alcmaeon.

The Athenians and Phormio put back from Acarnania, arrived at Naupactus, and sailed home to Athens in the spring. They took with them the ships they had captured, and those of the prisoners made in the recent actions who were freemen, and these were exchanged, man for man. And so ended this winter, and the third year of this war, of which Thucydides was the historian.
